judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: Footer link 'Opening Hours' to /node/65714, which redirects to /contact-us, titled 'Contact Us'. The claim is true about the title. But the live page body lists the council's opening hours: County Hall Monday-Thursday 9am-5pm, Friday 9am-4:30pm, the Civic Hub, Housing and Planning counters, and the Dundrum office hours. So the link leads to the opening hours its text promises, and Understanding 2.4.4 does not require the link text to match the page title. It passes. Rampa saw only the destination's title, not its content.

judgments.label: true_positive
judgments.rationale: [visual context] 'Find out more' button link (CSS uppercase) to the Transforming Dundrum project page. The visual label 'Transforming Dundrum:' is a <div> inside a styled <span>, not a heading, and the descriptive paragraphs are separate blocks. The link sits alone in its own div, with no title or aria-describedby. The nearest preceding heading is the unrelated news card h2 '€335 Million Budget Adopted...', which also precedes that card's own 'Find out more' link to a different page. So the purpose cannot be determined from the link and its programmatic context. Live HTML is the same. The claim names the failure.

judgments.label: true_positive
judgments.rationale: Top-menu link 'Gaeilge' (href #gaeilge, the Recite Me Irish-translation trigger) has no lang attribute and inherits lang=en. Understanding 3.1.2's 'Alternative language links' example gives exactly this pattern, a language's name written in that language, marked with lang. An English voice mispronounces 'Gaeilge', so the vernacular exception does not apply in practice. Live HTML has the same markup in both menus. The claim names the failure.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: An image that is all its link holds, linking to the event 'TradFest 2027' (live title checked). The image is a wordmark reading 'TradFest 2027 20-24 JAN', and its alt is 'tradfest wording'. Read as link text, the alt names TradFest, so users can tell the link goes to TradFest. By R2's first step it gives the link's purpose, and the claim that it does not say where the link leads is false. The alt is weak ('wording' is filler; the year and dates are left out), but that is not the failure claimed. Live HTML is the same.
